newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEP advocates more flexible EU cooperation.
newsitem.headline: MEP advocates more flexible EU cooperation.

text.p: The reform of the European Union treaty will be judged on the extent to which it increases cooperation between the EU member states, MEP Biagio de Giovanni has said.
The new head of the European Parliament's institutional affairs committee told reporters on Thursday that increasing cooperation was the most important aspect of EU treaty reform.
The Italian Socialist said member states who wanted to integrate more swiftly than others should be given a guarantee that their more recalcitrant neighbours would not hold them back.
He cited as an example Europe's planned economic and monetary union, which is not expected to involve all 15 member states in the initial stages.
The committee believed EU governments should have the initiative in deciding where greater cooperation was needed but the European Commission and the parliament should be consulted, de Giovanni said.

By contrast the committee thought it was a dangerous move to start introducing more flexible arrangements in areas which currently come under Community competence, such as free movements of goods, people, services and capital.
The MEP and professor of political philosophy said he agreed with an Irish proposal to give the EU the power to decide over some areas presently dealt with through inter-governmental cooperation.
For example, there had to be a minimum of common rules in the legal field to enable the member states to combat international crime.

The institutional affairs committee agreed there should be a change in the number of votes individual member states should have in the Council but had not yet worked out a precise formulae, de Giovanni said.
In an enlarged Union, it would be necessary to consider not just the number of countries voting but also the size of their population, the committee thought.
It would be inconceivable to have a situation where a number of states representing less than half the Union's population could impose their will on the rest, de Giovanni said.
